questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health economics, insurance, Ayushman Bharat & financing
questions.stem: Which term describes health expenditure that pushes a household below the poverty line?
options: Catastrophic health expenditure leading to impoverishment
questions.concept: Out-of-pocket payment at the point of care is the mechanism, which is why prepayment through tax funding or insurance and free drugs and diagnostics are the policy responses.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health economics, insurance, Ayushman Bharat & financing
questions.stem: Which measure of disease burden combines years of life lost from premature death with years lived with disability?
questions.concept: One DALY equals one lost year of healthy life, which allows fatal and non-fatal outcomes to be compared and priorities to be set across very different conditions.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health economics, insurance, Ayushman Bharat & financing
questions.stem: In an economic evaluation, which analysis expresses both costs and consequences in monetary terms?
questions.concept: Cost-effectiveness uses natural units such as cases prevented, cost-utility uses quality-adjusted life years, and cost-minimisation applies only when outcomes are known to be equivalent.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health economics, insurance, Ayushman Bharat & financing
questions.stem: Which component of Ayushman Bharat addresses comprehensive primary care rather than hospitalisation?
options: Health and wellness centres delivering an expanded twelve-service package
The Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana insurance scheme
questions.concept: The two pillars are deliberately complementary, with the wellness centres intended to reduce the need for hospitalisation that the insurance arm then funds.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health economics, insurance, Ayushman Bharat & financing
questions.stem: Which financing mechanism pays a provider a fixed amount per enrolled person per period regardless of services used?
questions.concept: Capitation contains cost and encourages prevention but risks under-provision and cherry-picking of healthy enrollees, whereas fee-for-service encourages over-provision.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health economics, insurance, Ayushman Bharat & financing
questions.stem: Which social insurance scheme in India covers organised-sector workers and their dependants through its own hospitals and dispensaries?
questions.concept: It is contributory, funded by employer and employee shares, and provides medical care plus cash benefits for sickness, maternity, disablement and dependants, distinguishing it from purely purchasing schemes.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health economics, insurance, Ayushman Bharat & financing
questions.stem: Why does a high proportion of out-of-pocket expenditure in total health spending indicate a weak health financing system?
options: It shifts financial risk to the individual at the moment of illness, deterring care-seeking and causing impoverishment
questions.concept: Risk pooling through prepayment is the defining function of a health financing system, so the share of pooled public expenditure is a core indicator of universal health coverage progress.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health planning, committees & health policy
questions.stem: Which national policy set the target of raising public health expenditure to 2.5 percent of gross domestic product?
questions.concept: The policy also set the goal of increasing state health spending to more than 8 percent of the state budget and emphasised assured comprehensive primary care as the route to universal health coverage.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health planning, committees & health policy
questions.stem: Which committee recommended the creation of the multipurpose health worker by integrating the roles of separate vertical programme workers?
questions.concept: Combining the malaria, smallpox, family planning and other single-purpose workers into one cadre was intended to improve efficiency and coverage at the village level.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health planning, committees & health policy
questions.stem: Which planning technique breaks a programme into activities with defined durations to identify the critical path and total time required?
options: Programme evaluation and review technique with critical path method
questions.concept: Identifying which activities cannot be delayed without delaying the whole project allows resources to be concentrated where slippage matters most.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health planning, committees & health policy
questions.stem: Which step comes first in the health planning cycle?
options: Analysis of the health situation to identify and prioritise problems
questions.concept: The cycle proceeds from situation analysis through setting objectives, assessing alternatives, programming, implementation and evaluation, and feeds back into a fresh analysis.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health planning, committees & health policy
questions.stem: Which committee recommended the establishment of a University of Health Sciences in every state and the development of a health manpower plan?
questions.concept: The committee addressed the mismatch between the numbers and types of health personnel produced and the needs of the service, proposing an integrated educational and manpower policy.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health planning, committees & health policy
questions.stem: Which indicator would best evaluate the process rather than the outcome of an antenatal care programme?
options: Proportion of pregnant women receiving four or more antenatal visits
questions.concept: Process indicators measure whether activities were delivered as planned and change quickly, whereas outcome indicators reflect the eventual health effect and respond slowly to programme change.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health planning, committees & health policy
questions.stem: Why are input and process indicators monitored alongside outcome indicators in a national programme?
options: Outcomes change slowly and are influenced by factors outside the programme, so process measures allow timely correction
Input indicators measure health status directly
Process indicators are cheaper to fabricate
questions.concept: Attributing a change in mortality to a programme requires long observation and control of confounders, so managers use the logic model of inputs, processes, outputs and outcomes together.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Planning and Management

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: Which Sustainable Development Goal is specifically concerned with health and wellbeing?
questions.concept: The health goal includes targets for maternal and child mortality, communicable and non-communicable disease, substance use, road injury, universal health coverage and reproductive health, and other goals on poverty, water and inequality act on health determinants.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. International Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: Which is the decision-making body of the World Health Organization, meeting annually in Geneva?
questions.concept: The Assembly of all member states sets policy and approves the budget, the Executive Board of elected members gives effect to its decisions, and the Secretariat under the Director-General carries out the work.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. International Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: In the disaster management cycle, which phase includes hazard mapping, building codes and early warning systems?
options: Mitigation and preparedness, before the event
questions.concept: Investment before an event reduces both mortality and cost far more than response after it, which is the central lesson of modern disaster management.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. International Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: Which of the following is the first priority in the immediate response phase after an earthquake?
options: Search and rescue with triage and treatment of the injured, and restoration of safe water
Mass immunisation against typhoid and cholera
questions.concept: Mass vaccination campaigns in the immediate aftermath divert resources from life-saving activity, and safe water, sanitation, shelter and surveillance prevent the epidemics that vaccination is feared for.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. International Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: Which triage category, using the standard colour code, denotes a casualty needing immediate life-saving intervention?
questions.concept: Yellow marks urgent but delayable care, green marks the walking wounded, and black or blue marks the dead or those with unsurvivable injury, and the aim of triage is the greatest good for the greatest number.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. International Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: Which international legal instrument obliges states to detect, assess, notify and respond to public health emergencies of international concern?
questions.concept: The regulations shifted from a list of specified diseases to any event that may constitute an emergency, and they require core surveillance and response capacities in every state party.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. International Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: International health, WHO, SDGs & disaster management
questions.stem: Why is disease surveillance strengthened rather than relaxed in the weeks after a natural disaster, even when no outbreak has occurred?
options: Displacement, crowding, damaged water and sanitation and interrupted immunisation raise the risk of outbreaks that early detection can contain
questions.concept: The classic post-disaster risks are diarrhoeal disease, measles, acute respiratory infection and vector-borne disease, and early warning systems with rapid response teams are what prevent them becoming epidemics.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. International Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Maternal health, RCH & safe motherhood programmes
questions.stem: How many antenatal visits does the current national guidance recommend as a minimum, and when does the first occur?
options: At least four visits, with the first in the first trimester
Two visits, both in the third trimester
questions.concept: India follows a minimum of four visits with registration in the first trimester, while WHO 2016 guidance recommends eight contacts, and the first-trimester visit permits dating, screening and early risk identification.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Maternal health, RCH & safe motherhood programmes
questions.stem: Which scheme provides a conditional cash transfer to promote institutional delivery among poor women?
questions.concept: Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram complements it by entitling every pregnant woman to free delivery including caesarean, drugs, diagnostics, diet and transport in public facilities.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Maternal health, RCH & safe motherhood programmes
questions.stem: Which iron and folic acid regimen is recommended for a non-anaemic pregnant woman under the national programme?
options: One tablet containing 60 mg elemental iron with 500 micrograms folic acid daily for at least 180 days from the second trimester, continued postpartum
Iron only in the third trimester
questions.concept: Anaemia Mukt Bharat sets out this schedule with a doubled dose for anaemic women, alongside deworming, testing and behaviour change, because anaemia is a major contributor to maternal death.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Maternal health, RCH & safe motherhood programmes
questions.stem: Which cause accounts for the largest share of direct maternal deaths in India?
questions.concept: Haemorrhage, mostly postpartum, is followed by sepsis and hypertensive disorders, which is why active management of the third stage, skilled attendance and prompt referral are the core interventions.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Maternal health, RCH & safe motherhood programmes
questions.stem: Which indicator measures the proportion of deliveries attended by a doctor, nurse or midwife and is a key process indicator for maternal survival?
questions.concept: Skilled attendance captures the competence available at the moment when most maternal deaths occur, and it is more informative than the place of delivery alone.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Maternal health, RCH & safe motherhood programmes
questions.stem: Which programme component addresses the largest remaining gap in maternal survival once institutional delivery is high?
options: Quality of intrapartum and immediate postpartum care, including management of complications and referral
Increasing the number of antenatal visits
questions.concept: Once women are delivering in facilities, deaths concentrate among those who reach care but do not receive timely, competent management, which is the rationale for LaQshya and the labour room quality initiative.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Maternal health, RCH & safe motherhood programmes
questions.stem: Why does the maternal mortality ratio remain a poor tool for monitoring progress in a single district year to year?
options: Maternal death is a rare event so small numbers give wide confidence intervals and unstable estimates
questions.concept: This is why process indicators, facility-based audits and confidential enquiry into maternal deaths are used locally, while the ratio is estimated at state and national level through the Sample Registration System.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: National health programs (NHM, NTEP, etc.)
questions.stem: Which programme provides free diagnostics, drugs and treatment for tuberculosis together with nutritional support by direct benefit transfer?
options: National Tuberculosis Elimination Programme with Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana
National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme
National Programme for Control of Blindness
questions.concept: Combining free diagnosis and treatment with cash for nutrition addresses the strong bidirectional link between tuberculosis and undernutrition, which is a major driver of incidence and poor outcomes in India.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. National Health Programmes

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: National immunization schedule
questions.stem: Which vaccines are given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks under the Universal Immunization Programme?
options: Pentavalent, oral polio, rotavirus and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, with fractional inactivated polio at 6 and 14 weeks
BCG, hepatitis B and oral polio
questions.concept: The primary series is compressed into the first months because protection is needed before maternal antibody wanes, and fractional inactivated polio is given intradermally at two of the three visits.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: National immunization schedule
questions.stem: At what age is the second dose of measles-rubella vaccine given in the national schedule?
questions.concept: The second dose covers primary vaccine failure from the 9-month dose, and it is given with the DPT and oral polio boosters and vitamin A at the same visit.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: National immunization schedule
questions.stem: Which vaccine is given only up to 1 year of age in the national schedule and is not given later?
options: BCG, which may be given up to 1 year if missed
questions.concept: Beyond 1 year the likelihood of prior natural infection or established immunity rises and the reaction is more marked, so BCG is not given as catch-up in older children in the programme.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: National immunization schedule
questions.stem: Which vaccine in the national schedule is given by the intradermal route?
options: BCG and fractional inactivated polio vaccine
questions.concept: Route errors are a recurrent cause of vaccine failure and adverse events, so knowing that pentavalent and pneumococcal are intramuscular, rotavirus and oral polio are oral, and measles-rubella is subcutaneous, matters practically.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: National immunization schedule
questions.stem: Which dose of tetanus and adult diphtheria toxoid is recommended for a pregnant woman with no previous immunisation record?
options: Two doses 4 weeks apart, with the second at least 4 weeks before delivery
questions.concept: A woman immunised in a previous pregnancy within the last 3 years receives a single booster, and maternal antibody crossing the placenta is what prevents neonatal tetanus.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: National immunization schedule
questions.stem: Which adverse event following immunisation is classified as a vaccine product-related reaction rather than a programme error?
options: Fever and local induration after pentavalent vaccine
Toxic shock from a contaminated multi-dose vial
Paralysis from injecting the wrong vaccine
questions.concept: Classification into product-related, quality defect, immunisation error, immunisation anxiety and coincidental events determines the corrective action, and errors point to training and logistics rather than to the vaccine itself.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: National immunization schedule
questions.stem: Why is the open vial policy applied to some vaccines but not to reconstituted BCG and measles-rubella?
options: Reconstituted vaccines contain no preservative and support contamination, so they are discarded within 4 hours or at the end of the session
questions.concept: Preservative-containing liquid vaccines such as oral polio, pentavalent, hepatitis B and tetanus toxoid may be used for up to 28 days if cold chain and labelling conditions are met, which reduces wastage substantially.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Immunization

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Non-communicable disease epidemiology: CVD, diabetes, cancer, tobacco
questions.stem: Which set of measures forms the WHO best buys for population-level non-communicable disease prevention?
options: Tobacco and alcohol taxation, salt reduction, restriction of trans fats and promotion of physical activity
Mass screening of the whole adult population
questions.concept: These interventions are cost-effective and act on the whole distribution of risk, which yields more prevented events than treating only high-risk individuals, the prevention paradox described by Rose.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Chronic Non-communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Non-communicable disease epidemiology: CVD, diabetes, cancer, tobacco
questions.stem: Under the national programme, opportunistic screening for hypertension, diabetes and common cancers is offered from what age?
options: 30 years and above, at health and wellness centres
questions.concept: Population-based screening under the NP-NCD covers hypertension, diabetes and oral, breast and cervical cancer, delivered with a community-based assessment checklist for risk stratification.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Chronic Non-communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Non-communicable disease epidemiology: CVD, diabetes, cancer, tobacco
questions.stem: Which tobacco control measure has the strongest evidence for reducing consumption, especially among the young?
options: Significant increases in tobacco taxation and price
questions.concept: Demand is price-elastic and more so in adolescents and low-income groups, which is why the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control places taxation first among demand-reduction measures.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Chronic Non-communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Non-communicable disease epidemiology: CVD, diabetes, cancer, tobacco
questions.stem: Which cancer is the commonest among Indian women, and what is the principal screening approach in the national programme?
options: Breast cancer, screened by clinical breast examination at the community level
Cervical cancer, screened by HPV DNA testing of all women
questions.concept: Breast cancer has overtaken cervical cancer as the commonest female cancer in India, and the programme uses clinical breast examination with referral because mammographic screening is not feasible at scale.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Chronic Non-communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Non-communicable disease epidemiology: CVD, diabetes, cancer, tobacco
questions.stem: Which risk factor accounts for the largest attributable share of oral cancer in India?
options: Smokeless tobacco and areca nut chewing
questions.concept: Because the exposure is visible and the lesion is accessible, oral cancer is one of the few malignancies where community-based visual screening by trained workers has been shown to reduce mortality in high-risk groups.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Chronic Non-communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Non-communicable disease epidemiology: CVD, diabetes, cancer, tobacco
questions.stem: Which measure of population salt intake is recommended by WHO as a target to reduce cardiovascular disease?
options: Less than 5 grams of salt, or 2 grams of sodium, per person per day
questions.concept: Achieving it requires reformulation of processed food and front-of-pack labelling as well as consumer education, because most salt in an increasingly processed diet is added before purchase.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Chronic Non-communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Non-communicable disease epidemiology: CVD, diabetes, cancer, tobacco
questions.stem: In the epidemiological transition, what pattern characterises a country like India today?
options: A double burden, with communicable disease still substantial while non-communicable disease and injury dominate overall mortality
Neither, as mortality is dominated by injury
questions.concept: The transition is also unequal within the country, so programmes must simultaneously sustain infectious disease control and build chronic care systems, which is the central challenge of health system design.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Chronic Non-communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Non-communicable disease epidemiology: CVD, diabetes, cancer, tobacco
questions.stem: Why does a high-risk approach alone fail to reduce the population burden of cardiovascular disease?
options: Most events arise from the large number of people at modest risk rather than the small number at high risk, the prevention paradox
High-risk individuals do not benefit from treatment
questions.concept: Rose's insight is that a small shift in the whole distribution prevents more events than intensive treatment of the tail, which is why population and high-risk approaches are complementary rather than alternatives.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Chronic Non-communicable Diseases
